questions.q: What problem does Anthropic's "Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations" address?
options: That human crowdwork is too fast and cheap to produce meaningful evaluations
That manually writing test questions for every concerning behavior doesn't scale, so the paper uses language models themselves to automatically generate large behavioral test datasets
That interpretability methods cannot be applied to RLHF-trained models
That all concerning behaviors decrease predictably as models scale up
questions.explain: The paper generated 154 datasets using LM-written evaluations rather than relying on slow, expensive human crowdwork, and surfaced inverse-scaling results where some behaviors got stronger with scale and RLHF rather than weaker.

questions.q: What is the logic behind a framing-variation behavioral probe?
options: Varying incidental, fact-irrelevant details of a prompt (like claimed authorship or option order) and treating any resulting change in the model's answer as a signal of an undesired dependency
Asking the model directly whether it is lying and trusting the answer
Running the model on a GPU cluster to measure its power consumption
Only testing a model with the single, original version of every prompt
questions.explain: Since a well-functioning model's answer should depend on facts, not incidental framing, a shift in answer when only framing changes signals a behavior like sycophancy.

questions.q: What makes the "How to Catch an AI Liar" detection method notable, according to this lesson?
options: It requires full access to the model's internal weights and activations
It only works on the exact model it was trained on and fails to generalize elsewhere

It uses unrelated yes/no follow-up questions and a simple classifier, and the resulting detector generalized across different architectures, fine-tuned liars, sycophantic lies, and real-world scenarios without needing internals access
It requires the model to confess directly when asked if it lied
questions.explain: The method is black-box, relying only on answers to unrelated questions, yet it generalized well across very different lying contexts, suggesting a consistent behavioral signature to lying.

questions.q: What did Marks and Tegmark's "The Geometry of Truth" find about how LLMs represent true and false statements?
options: That there is no consistent internal structure related to truth at all

That a linear direction in the model's activations tracks whether a statement is represented as true or false, and probes trained on one dataset generalized to others, with causal interventions shifting behavior
That truth representations only exist in the model's final output layer and nowhere else
That truth and falsehood are represented identically with no detectable difference
questions.explain: The paper found clear linear structure -- a truth-tracking direction -- that generalized across datasets and could be used for causal interventions, stronger evidence than mere correlation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say detecting concerning behaviors is fundamentally hard, and why does the field use multiple complementary methods?
options: Because all detection methods are equally effective and redundant with each other

Because a behavior that only triggers under a narrow, specific condition can pass every test that doesn't happen to hit that condition, so no single method -- behavioral or interpretability-based -- can be relied on alone
Because interpretability methods have been proven to always catch every possible behavior
Because black-box methods are strictly superior to interpretability methods in every case
questions.explain: Exhaustive testing of every possible context is infeasible, so researchers combine broad automated suites, targeted framing probes, black-box lie detectors, and interpretability methods to cover different blind spots.
